card.title: Combustion of benzene (free combustion only) and uses

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Benzene burns as 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O — exothermic and oxygen-hungry, with a luminous sooty flame that is the 1 : 1 H : C ratio made visible in glowing carbon particles. Its uses split by the property exploited: non-polarity (solvent), substitution and addition chemistry (styrene, phenol, aniline, nylon precursors), anti-knock value (restricted fuel).…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Burning Benzene and Using It Benzene's combustion is the sooty-flame exemplar: **2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O**, highly exothermic but incomplete in ordinary flames because the ring is 92.3% carbon. Its uses follow its properties: solvent, precursor to styrene/phenol/cyclohexane, and — increasingly restricted — fuel additive.  ·  ## 2. Theorem Mirror - **Combustion equation:** 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O + heat (ΔH ≈ −3268 kJ per 2 mol). - **Flame character:** luminous, smoky (sooty) — the C : H ratio (1 : 1) leaves carbon unoxidised in the flame's fuel-rich interior; the soot is elemental carbon escaping before full combustion. - **Generalisation:** aromatic and high-carbon fuels burn smoky; the flame is a composition readout.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Balance 2C6H6 + 15O2 -> 12CO2 + 6H2O once, carefully - the 15 is the number examiners check.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (5m): Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of benzene and explain why it burns with a smoky flame.** — **Equation:** 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O + heat (check: C 12 = 12; H 12 = 12; O 30 = 24 + 6 ✓).…  ·  **NEB-style (6m): Compare the flames of burning benzene (C6H6) and cyclohexane (C6H12), and justify the difference using composition.** — **Benzene:** H : C = 6 : 6 = 1 ⟹ oxygen-hungry, fuel-rich zones common ⟹ **luminous, heavily sooty flame**.…

rows.text: Categorise uses (solvent / precursor / fuel) rather than listing - the structure earns the organisation mark.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The sooty flame is local stoichiometry deficit made visible - glowing carbon particles escaping before full oxidation.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: 2C6H6 + 15O2 -> 12CO2 + 6H2O, highly exothermic; luminous sooty flame from C:H = 1:1 - fuel-rich zones release glowing carbon particles. H:C ratio predicts flame cleanliness (cyclohexane cleaner, benzene smokier).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Benzene is a proven human carcinogen - its solvent and fuel uses are legally restricted; toluene substitutes.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (6m): List the important uses of benzene, grouped by the property or reaction each use exploits.** — **Solvent uses (exploit non-polarity):** dissolves resins, fats, waxes, iodine, sulphur — the dispersion-contact champion of the early chemical industry.…  ·  **NEB-style (5m): Calculate the heat released when 78 g of benzene is completely burnt, given that the enthalpy of combustion of benzene is -3268 kJ per mole of reaction as written (2 mol C6H6).** — **Moles:** 78 g / 78 g/mol = 1 mol C₆H₆.…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Deep Conceptual — The Sooty Flame as Stoichiometry Made Visible - The balanced equation demands 15 O₂ per 2 benzene — an oxygen-hungry ratio. In a real flame the fuel-rich zones cannot supply that oxygen locally, so carbon is released as fine particles before reaching CO₂; these particles glow incandescently (luminous yellow) and deposit as soot.…  ·  ```svg From benzene to everyday materials — the uses chain <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" font-family="Segoe UI" font-size="14"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="300" fill="#ffffff"/><circle cx="320" cy="80" r="40" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="3"/><text x="320" y="85" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1d4ed8" font-size="15">C₆H₆</text><g font-size="13"…  ·  ### Deep dive — combustion arithmetic and the uses list that follows structure Complete combustion: 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O, ΔH ≈ −3268 kJ/mol of benzene (high fuel value). Incomplete combustion in a limited oxygen supply gives the luminous, smoky flame: free carbon particles (soot) form because the C:H ratio (1:1) is far richer in carbon than an alkane's (1:3).…
